pull.title: fuzz: report more events, and check more invariants in connman target
pull.body:
On top of #36765, this extends FuzzedSock to report more events a real OS could report (see #36737 for some coverage of those), and improves the connman fuzz target to assert more socket handling invariants.

The first commit is also a fix to uniquely identify sockets, as currently each socket can only use one of two descriptor values, which means the fuzz target would act on one peer with the event of another.

See commit messages for details.

events.message:
fuzz: give each FuzzedSock its own socket

Prior to this commit, every FuzzedSock had one of two socket values and
CConnman::SocketHandler() merged the entries of different peers in a
single wait, which led the connman fuzz target to act on one peer with
the events of another.

This fixes it by using a different descriptor value for each socket,
like the OS does for real sockets. This is achieved by numbering the
sockets down from a global counter, restarted before each fuzz input to
keep each run deterministic.

A sanity check is added to CheckGlobalsImpl, in the same fashion as the
it's done for the global PRNG and mocked time states.

fuzz: let FuzzedSock waits report what the real OS can report

FuzzedSock::Wait() and WaitMany() reported either nothing or exactly the
requested events. The real OS reports more than that, and the fuzz
targets never exercised the callers on it:
- only some of the requested events, e.g. SendEvent alone on an idle
  connection;
- ErrorEvent, with or without RecvEvent, to a socket that requested
  RecvEvent, as select() does for urgent data;
- a failed connection, e.g. a reset one: poll() reports it as
  ErrorEvent whatever was requested, even nothing.

Model these. A failed connection stays failed: waits keep reporting
it, Recv() returns at most what was buffered before (a bounded amount
picked when it fails) and then fails for good, and Send() fails. So a
socket that did not request RecvEvent can be read from only once its
connection failed, and only for a bounded amount, as on the real OS.

WaitMany() now picks the outcome per socket, so that each socket keeps
its own state. As before, the requested events occur when the fuzz
input is exhausted, so that waits do not go on forever.

fuzz: assert more invariants in the connman target

Flag a number of events in the FuzzedSock and assert corresponding
invariants after running the handler.

comments.body:
style-nit: I guess this works, but design-wise this struct was more meant to be a no-op linter (only crash on a bug), not a behavior-changing cleanup utility 😅 

Either:

* Add a `g_used_socket` and `g_reset_socket` (and use it to lint and enforce a call to `ResetFuzzedSockets` in the affected fuzz targets)
* Just add `ResetFuzzedSockets` in the affected fuzz targets and hope it is sufficient without a linter
* Leave it as-is

Up to you.

Happy to change this, but i'm not sure how CheckGlobalsImpl() is a no-op linter? It is already resetting state that fuzz targets depend on. Resetting the starting descriptor value for created sockets does not seem that different from resetting the mock time(s).

The idea is that this is resetting the mock time, so that system time is used. However, if system time was used, it would fail the fuzz run due to non-determinism.

Conversely, if the two time-clear toggles were removed, the fuzz run would just run normally and still deterministically, because all fuzz targets set their mock time explicitly.

This is just a style preference of mine to have each test case fully list all dependencies or requirements by itself, so that it is self-contained and doesn't depend on implicit global setup.
Make sense, i'll move the Reset to targets making use of fuzzed sockets then.
Done, along with a sanity check akin to that used for the global PRNG / mocked time states.

I think that the `continue` here is right for the fail-closed checks, but it also skips the readiness, `m_recv_twice` and `m_send_after_short` checks. Those describe what the handler did during the run, whether or not the socket survived. 

The problem is that the bugs these checks look for usually end with the handler closing the socket. For example, a read without RecvEvent on a healthy FuzzedSock mostly returns 0 or an error, and the handler then calls CloseSocketDisconnect(). The node now has no socket, so the check never runs. The violation is only seen when the bad read happens to return data.

I tested this with a mutant that also reads on SendEvent:

```diff
diff --git a/src/net.cpp b/src/net.cpp
index f31604f6c5..b781371074 100644
--- a/src/net.cpp
+++ b/src/net.cpp
@@ -2218,7 +2218,7 @@ void CConnman::SocketHandlerConnected(const std::vector<CNode*>& nodes,
             }
         }

-        if (recvSet || errorSet)
+        if (recvSet || errorSet || sendSet)
         {
             // typical socket buffer is 8K-64K
             uint8_t pchBuf[0x10000];
```

My clanker suggests to keep a reference to each socket before the handler runs, check behaviour on that reference, and only tie the fail-closed checks to whether the node still holds it.
